Well, to be honest, it’s... it’s just been a really overwhelming couple of weeks. I work as a mechanic at this auto shop downtown, mostly dealing with heavy-duty stuff, you know, trucks, SUVs, that kind of thing. I've been there a while and I know my way around a garage, but... well, what brought me in is that I keep hearing this voice. 

It’s a man’s voice. And I know how that sounds, but it’s not like a faint thought in my head or just my imagination playing tricks on me. It is as clear as somebody standing right next to me holding a socket wrench. I'll be working in my bay, just trying to get my hours in, and I hear him coming straight out of the garage vents. We have these massive industrial vents up near the ceiling for the exhaust fumes, and his voice just travels right down through the metal. Or sometimes—and this is the part that really messes with my head—I’ll pop the hood on a vehicle to check an alternator or do a routine inspection, and the voice comes right from under the hood. Just... right out of the engine bay. 

And he just talks and talks. He keeps telling me not to trust my husband, just going on about how my husband is plotting things and I need to watch my back with him. And then he’ll switch and start telling me not to touch certain cars. Like, the service advisor will roll a car into my bay for a diagnostic, and the voice will tell me I absolutely cannot touch that specific car, like it's dangerous or something. It’s making it impossible to do my job because I'm just standing there staring at a manifold, listening to this guy tell me my marriage is a lie and I can't do my work, and... I just don't know how to make it stop.

It’s making it impossible to do my job because I'm just standing there staring at a manifold, listening to this guy tell me my marriage is a lie and I can't do my work, and... I just don't know how to make it stop.\n\nDoctor: Does the voice ever tell you to do something, rather than just telling you not to do something or warning you about your husband?\n\nPatient: No, no, it’s not really like that. It’s like this constant, heavy blanket of... of warnings, just suffocating me. \n\nLike, I’ll be standing there, wiping my hands on a shop towel, just trying to take a five-minute breather between jobs, and he’s not saying \"go confront your husband\" or \"go smash that windshield.\" It’s more like... \"don't go home tonight, he's waiting for you, he's got a plan.\" And it just spins and spins in my head. I'll just be staring at my socket sets, completely frozen. So, no, he doesn't tell me to *do* things... it's just... it's always pulling me away from living my life, if that makes sense. I loved the community, the chatting, the feeling of being involved and doing something good. But lately? Lately, I just... I can't even make myself care. 

There are these long stretches where I don't even go. I just skip the potlucks entirely. People will call me, you know, the ladies from church leaving voicemails, asking where I've been, if I'm still bringing my potato salad, and I just... I don't call anyone back. I stare at my phone while it rings, and I just can't muster the energy to pick it up. It feels like such a monumental effort just to say hello. 

And it's not just church. It's everything. Even at work, which I used to take so much pride in. I mean, I'm a good mechanic. I love the satisfaction of fixing a problem, of getting an engine running smooth again. But now, I'll just sit there in the bay, or even at home in my living room, and I'll just stare. Like, I'll literally just sit and stare at my tools, my ratchets and my torque wrenches, and I just feel nothing. I can't make myself care about the cars, I can't make myself care about the church, I can't even make myself care about calling my friends back. It's just this heavy, blank feeling. It's like I'm hollowed out. And honestly, it's terrifying, because I know I should care, I know I used to care, but the feeling is just... gone. It's just completely gone, and I don't know how to get it back.

Well, yeah... I mean, I know I just brought all that up, but yes, I absolutely believe it's real. Because it is real. I'm not... I'm not just making it up or imagining it like a daydream, if that's what you're getting at. 

You have to understand, when you work in a service bay, you get used to a very specific set of noises. You've got pneumatic impact wrenches going off, air compressors kicking on, the bay doors rattling, radios blaring... you learn how to filter out the background noise so you can hear the important stuff, like a rod knocking or a bearing whining. But this voice... it cuts right through all of that shop noise. Like I was explaining, it's the whole reason I'm sitting here talking to you. I keep hearing this man’s voice, and it's not some fuzzy thought in the back of my mind. It has a physical location. 

When it comes from the garage vents, I can literally hear the acoustics of it, like the sound waves are bouncing off the galvanized steel of the ductwork. And when I pop a hood and it's coming from the engine bay... I mean, it is as clear as somebody standing right next to me. Clearer, honestly, because half the guys I work with mumble. But this man doesn't mumble. He speaks with total authority. When he's telling me not to trust my husband, or when he's explicitly warning me not to touch certain cars, I can hear the pitch of his voice, the tone, even the breath behind the words. 

If it wasn't real, how could I hear it so clearly over a running engine? How could it startle me so badly that I physically drop my ratchet? People think that if you hear something that isn't supposed to be there, it must feel like a dream. But it doesn't. It's solid. It's as real as the grease on my hands. I've actually caught myself walking circles around a vehicle, checking the blind spots around the hydraulic lift, looking behind the big Snap-on toolboxes, because I am completely convinced there is a physical human being hiding in my work area playing a sick joke on me. But there's never anyone there. It's just the voice. 

But it's coming from right there, right out of the intake manifold or the radiator fan, just plain as day, telling me all these awful things. So, yes, doctor, I believe it's real. I have to believe it's real because my own two ears are hearing it happen, shift after shift. I wouldn't be taking time off work and sitting in a psychiatrist's office if I didn't know for a fact that I was really hearing it.

No, never. I mean, before this started? Absolutely not. I had a completely normal life. I've never had any weird perceptions, or heard anything that wasn't there, or experienced anything even remotely like this in my entire life. 

But this current situation... the voices and the tracking beliefs, they've been happening for about ten months now. But yeah, all of it—the voice in the shop, the feeling that I'm being monitored and tracked—it's been about ten solid months.

It was right at the tail end of winter, right as we were finally getting out of the rush of swapping out snow tires and moving into spring maintenance. I was doing a heater core replacement on a 2015 Chevy Silverado—which, if you know anything about modern trucks, means you basically have to pull the entire dashboard out just to get to it, it is a massive, incredibly frustrating job that takes hours. I was deep under the dash, my hands were cramped, and that was the very first time I heard the man's voice. And it was right around that exact same time that I started noticing the signs that I was being tracked, like someone was monitoring my route home from the garage. 

So it's been ten months of this. And ten months might not sound like a long time in the grand scheme of a whole life, but when you are going to work every single day and you feel like you have to check the wheel wells of your own truck for GPS monitors, and you have a man yelling out of a radiator that your husband is a liar... ten months feels like an absolute eternity. I haven't had a single moment of real peace since it started. I'm just exhausted. But before that Silverado ten months ago? No. Never. Nothing like this ever happened to me before.

Well, I mean... no, not really. I know I just said it sounds far-fetched, and part of me—like, the logical part of my brain that knows how to diagnose a misfire or rebuild a transmission—that part knows how crazy it sounds to someone else. But doubt it? No. I don't doubt it.

So, yeah, it's external. It has to be external. I just... I don't know how he's doing it, or how he's hiding from me, but it's definitely not my own mind. It's a real voice, out loud, in the shop.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself having trouble expressing your thoughts in a coherent and logical manner?\n\nPatient: No, I don't think so. I mean, I know I'm talking a lot right now, and I know I have a tendency to really get into the weeds with the details, but... no, I don't have trouble making sense. My thoughts are perfectly logical. They have to be, you know? \n\nIn my line of work, if you can't explain your diagnostic process clearly, you're not going to last very long. Like, if I'm doing an inspection and I find that the brake calipers are seizing up, I can't just go to the service writer and spout a bunch of jumbled nonsense. I have to explain exactly what I found, step by step, so they can translate that to the customer and get the repair authorized. I have to be able to say, look, the slide pins are rusted out, the pads are wearing unevenly because of it, and the rotor is completely glazed, so we need to replace the whole assembly. It has to be a straight line from A to B to C. \n\nSo my brain works in a very systematic way. I'm always putting things in order. Even with everything going on right now, with this man's voice yelling at me from the radiators and the stress it's putting on me, I feel like I'm laying it all out for you very clearly, aren't I? I'm not... I'm not losing my train of thought or speaking in riddles or anything like that. I know exactly what I want to say, and I say it. It's just that I have a lot to say right now because this whole situation with the voice is so incredibly overwhelming and it's taking up so much of my energy. \n\nBut as far as being coherent? My heart starts pounding out of my chest, my hands get sweaty, and I just stand there staring at the engine block because I don't know what will happen if I actually touch the car after he warned me not to. \n\nSo, yes, it causes a massive amount of anxiety. I can't work, I can't trust my husband, I can't even open a hood without bracing myself for what this man is going to say to me. It's just completely taken over my day-to-day life, and I couldn't handle the panic anymore, which is exactly why I finally made the appointment to come in.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any traumatic events in your past?\n\nPatient: No, I mean... when you say traumatic, I usually think of, like, being in a war, or being in some horrible, catastrophic car wreck. And I've seen the aftermath of some really bad wrecks towed into the shop, believe me. Just last year, we had this Ford Explorer brought in that was completely crushed on the driver's side, just folded up like an accordion. The tow truck driver told me the guy somehow walked away without a scratch, which is an absolute miracle when you looked at the frame damage. But me personally? No. I've never been in a crash like that. \n\nI actually had a pretty standard, normal life, I guess. I just liked working with my hands too much, you know? My dad was always tinkering out in the garage when I was a kid, and I'd always be right out there with him, holding the flashlight. He'd always get frustrated and yell at me to hold it steady—you know how dads are, always saying, \"Keep the light on the bolt, not in my eyes!\"—but that's not trauma. That's just growing up. I sit here and I try to rack my brain, trying to think if there's some hidden, awful thing in my past that would explain all this. Like, I keep wondering if there's a reason why my brain feels so heavy and empty, or why there's suddenly a grown man's voice coming out from under the hood of a Honda Civic telling me my husband is a liar. But... there's just nothing. My life was completely normal. Boring, even! It was just church, the shop, and home. So no, no trauma. Honestly, a part of me almost wishes there was something, because then at least there would be a reason for why this is happening to me, you know? Like a cause and effect. But no, I haven't been through anything like that.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe the voice you're hearing is real and actually coming from the vents or under the hood of cars?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah... I mean, I know I just brought all that up, but yes, I absolutely believe it's real. Because it is real. I'm not... I'm not just making it up or imagining it like a daydream, if that's what you're getting at. \n\nYou have to understand, when you work in a service bay, you get used to a very specific set of noises. You've got pneumatic impact wrenches going off, air compressors kicking on, the bay doors rattling, radios blaring... you learn how to filter out the background noise so you can hear the important stuff, like a rod knocking or a bearing whining. But this voice... it cuts right through all of that shop noise. Like I was explaining, it's the whole reason I'm sitting here talking to you. I keep hearing this man’s voice, and it's not some fuzzy thought in the back of my mind. It has a physical location. \n\nWhen it comes from the garage vents, I can literally hear the acoustics of it, like the sound waves are bouncing off the galvanized steel of the ductwork. And when I pop a hood and it's coming from the engine bay... I mean, it is as clear as somebody standing right next to me. Clearer, honestly, because half the guys I work with mumble. But this man doesn't mumble. He speaks with total authority. When he's telling me not to trust my husband, or when he's explicitly warning me not to touch certain cars, I can hear the pitch of his voice, the tone, even the breath behind the words. \n\nIf it wasn't real, how could I hear it so clearly over a running engine? How could it startle me so badly that I physically drop my ratchet? People think that if you hear something that isn't supposed to be there, it must feel like a dream. But it doesn't. It's solid. It's as real as the grease on my hands. But there's never anyone there. It's just the voice. \n\nBut it's coming from right there, right out of the intake manifold or the radiator fan, just plain as day, telling me all these awful things. So, yes, doctor, I believe it's real. I have to believe it's real because my own two ears are hearing it happen, shift after shift. I wouldn't be taking time off work and sitting in a psychiatrist's office if I didn't know for a fact that I was really hearing it.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used recreational drugs or alcohol to the point where it interfered with your daily life?\n\nPatient: Oh, no. No, definitely not. I mean, I know there's this whole stereotype about mechanics, right? People think we all just clock out at five, crack open a twelve-pack of cheap beer, and sit around on overturned buckets in the parking lot until the sun goes down. I'm standing under vehicles that weigh thousands of pounds, suspended in the air by hydraulic lifts. I'm dealing with highly pressurized lines, volatile chemicals, and heavy machinery. If you are hungover, or high, or even just a little fuzzy from a few too many drinks the night before, you could literally kill yourself or someone else in the bay next to you. You miss one safety latch on the hoist, or you forget to torque a lug nut to the right spec, and it's an absolute disaster waiting to happen. So I take that really, really seriously. I don't have any kind of substance problem. I almost wish I did, because then you could just tell me to go to rehab and this whole nightmare would stop. You know, like when you read a book to yourself and you hear your own voice in your head? But this isn't that. This is a man.
